from pypdf import PdfReader

strengths: The task addresses a meaningful gap between audio-visual semantic segmentation and video instance segmentation: distinguishing individual sounding objects, including instances of the same category, while maintaining identities across time. This is a useful contribution to multimodal video understanding.

AVISeg represents a substantial annotation contribution: 926 videos averaging 61.4 seconds, 56,871 annotated frames, and 94,074 instance masks across 26 categories. Its mixture of silent, single-source, and multi-source frames supports evaluating sound-dependent segmentation and tracking.

The baseline has quantitative support beyond the proposed metric. Under the shared ResNet-50 and training-iteration setup, AVISM achieves 61.73 HOTA and 40.57 mAP, compared with VITA's 57.48/36.25 and COMBO's 57.39/37.84 (Table 2). These improvements provide evidence for the usefulness of the audio-visual adaptation.

Table 4 supports both fusion stages: adding frame-level fusion increases HOTA from 57.48 to 59.59, and adding video-level fusion increases it to 61.73. Window-size and backbone ablations provide additional practical information. The supplement documents training settings, baseline prompts, and informative failure cases involving similar sounding instances.
weaknesses: FSLA is not reproducibly specified. Algorithm 1 unconditionally credits silent frames, omits the stated category and object-count checks, and initializes counters outside the IoU-threshold loop. It also lacks the class averaging described in Section 3.2. These discrepancies affect the definition of a central benchmark metric. They do not establish that the reported implementation is wrong, but the manuscript leaves that implementation unresolved; HOTA and mAP provide separate supporting evidence.

The evidence for annotation reliability is incomplete. Section 4 describes SAM-assisted annotation and repeated manual review, but does not explain how annotators resolve ambiguous overlapping sounds, attribute similar sounds to individual instances, or verify identities across silent intervals. No agreement or quantitative annotation audit is reported. These details matter because correct sound attribution, beyond mask quality, defines the new task.

The large-model conclusions exceed what the adaptations establish. Section 11 selects only the top audio category for Sam4AVS and treats same-category masks as one instance for Sam4AVS/BuboGPT; AL-Ref-SAM 2 likewise treats each category as one instance. These adapters structurally prevent representing some central AVIS cases. Table 3 demonstrates limitations of these particular zero-shot pipelines, but does not cleanly isolate the underlying models' instance discrimination or temporal reasoning.

The experiments do not directly quantify several defining challenges. There is no dedicated evaluation of multiple same-category sources, identity recovery after silence, or performance versus sequence duration. The multi-source aggregate includes different-category sources, and Table 5 measures processing capacity rather than accuracy on progressively longer videos. Sampling at 1 FPS also limits conclusions about precise sound onset and offset localization.

Architectural originality is modest: object-token association, shifted-window processing, query decoding, and matching losses largely follow Mask2Former/VITA and related work. The principal contribution is the task and dataset, supported by a useful baseline. Some baseline reproduction details remain unclear, particularly how AVSS methods obtain consistent instance identities while allegedly retaining their original losses and training procedures.
